documents.text: Refunds are processed within five to seven business days after approval. Refund requests must include the original transaction reference.
Enterprise plans include single sign-on, audit logs, and role based access control. Administrators can manage organization members.
The standard API rate limit is 100 requests per minute per tenant. Burst traffic may receive HTTP 429 responses.
Critical incidents must be escalated to the on-call engineer immediately. The incident commander coordinates mitigation and communication.
Production deployments require a successful automated test suite and an approved change record before release.
Data retention defaults to 30 days for application logs. Enterprise customers may request a longer retention period.
Refund status updates appear in the billing portal after approval. Failed refunds are retried by the payment processor.
API authentication uses signed bearer tokens. Requests without valid credentials return HTTP 401.
Incident postmortems should document impact, timeline, root cause, and corrective actions within five business days.
Standard plans provide email support. Enterprise plans add SSO, audit logs, advanced access controls, and priority support.
Deployments are rolled out gradually using canary release. Rollback is available when health checks fail.
Application logs may contain request identifiers and operational metadata. Sensitive payloads should not be logged.
Rate limits can differ by plan and tenant. A temporary burst allowance does not change the configured sustained quota.
A refund may be rejected when the transaction reference is missing or the request falls outside the refund policy.
The incident commander owns operational coordination while the on-call engineer performs immediate technical response.
